title: Justinian Institutes wild-control operator with nature-dependent reference scope
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED, NOT SELECTED. Justinian Institutes II.12–16 gives a connected ownership account for wild animals, wounded animals, bees, returning tame-wild animals, and domestic chickens/geese. One finite CONTROL_LOSS operator resolves the same visible escape/pursuit context differently according to the source-bound NATURE and RETURN_INTENT fields: a wild animal that recovers natural freedom goes to the first occupant, while a domestic fowl remains its owner's property even out of sight. The constructor also preserves the source's adopted rule that wounding without actual capture does not create ownership.

source.source_span: II.12 wild capture, custody, escape and first occupant; II.13 wounded animal and competing opinions; II.14 bees, hive and swarm; II.15 peacocks, pigeons and tame deer; II.16 domestic chickens and geese.
source.provenance: Scott's public English translation of the Institutes is used as the source-owned clause witness; the Digest Book 41 parallel is checked for the same wild-animal and pursuit distinctions. No Latin target vocabulary or specific manuscript witness is claimed.

duplicate_screen.checked: IDEA000395/IDEA000400 Justinian sale and contract state; IDEA000425 Cato attached propagation; IDEA000449 Hippocratic feedback; IDEA000451 Cicero conditional duty; prior wild-animal/possession searches and route-check.
duplicate_screen.difference: The retained Justinian card concerns sale price, delivery, title, and accidental risk. This card concerns a single control-loss operator whose reference target changes with legal nature, visibility, pursuit difficulty, enclosure, and return intention; it includes a same-surface escape contrast between wild and domestic animals.

presuppositions: An animal's legal nature is a source-bound field: wild, tame-wild with a return habit, bee, or domestic fowl.
Ownership can persist through custody, visibility/pursuit, or return intention, but these are not the same physical identity condition.
First occupant means the first later person who secures the animal after the source-defined loss of the prior owner's control.
Wounding severe enough to permit capture is not the same source event as actual seizure; the adopted opinion rejects ownership before seizure.
Entry on another person's land can be prohibited even where taking the wild animal would otherwise create ownership.

clauses.content: Wild beasts, birds, and fish become the captor's property when taken; natural law gives an ownerless thing to the first possessor.
The place of capture, the hunter's own land or another's, does not change acquisition, but the landowner may forbid entry when aware of the intended hunt.
After capture, ownership lasts while custody is retained; escape plus recovery of natural freedom ends it and gives the animal to the first later captor.
Natural freedom is recognized when the animal leaves sight, or remains visible but becomes difficult to pursue.

A severely wounded animal that can be captured raises two opinions: Trebatius grants ownership while pursuit continues and removes it when pursuit stops; the confirmed opinion grants no ownership until actual seizure because intervening events may prevent capture.
Bees are wild; settling on a tree does not make them the tree owner's property until enclosed in a hive, and another person who encloses them becomes owner.

Honey made by bees may be taken without theft, subject to the landowner's right to forbid entry; a swarm escaped from a hive remains the owner's while visible and not difficult to pursue, otherwise the first occupant owns it.
Peacocks, pigeons, and tame deer remain wild by nature; for an animal accustomed to depart and return, ownership lasts while it intends to return, and ends when it abandons that habit.
Chickens and geese are domestic rather than wild; if frightened and flying beyond sight, they remain their owner's property, and a profitable taker commits theft.

complete_examples.reference_change: The later first-occupant reference replaces the original captor after natural freedom; the original animal identity remains continuous.
The same out-of-sight escape does not redirect ownership because domestic nature changes the control-loss rule; the later taker is an offender, not the new owner.
Pursuit after wounding does not supply the adopted seizure event; Trebatius' owner-while-pursuing rival would output ALICE.

global_rules: If nature=WILD and the animal is captured, claimant owns while custody is retained; if it escapes and is no longer visible or pursuit is difficult, FIRST_OCCUPANT becomes owner.
If nature=WILD and wounded but not seized, the adopted Justinian rule yields NO_OWNER_UNTIL_CAPTURE; the Trebatius pursuit rule is retained only as a named rival.
If nature=BEE, tree settlement alone yields no ownership; enclosure yields ownership, and escaped swarms use visibility plus pursuit difficulty as the loss boundary.
If nature=TAME_WILD, departure does not end ownership while RETURN_INTENT remains true; abandoning the return habit redirects ownership to FIRST_OCCUPANT.
If nature=DOMESTIC, escape beyond sight does not redirect ownership; a profitable later taker triggers THEFT instead.
Land-entry permission is a separate constraint on the acquisition event and cannot be silently folded into ownership identity.
constructor.observable_consequence: The same visible context—capture followed by escape beyond sight—produces a changed owner/reference when NATURE changes from WILD to DOMESTIC. The wounded case independently changes the result when WOUND is present without SEIZE: adopted law yields no owner, while the named Trebatius rival assigns the pursuing claimant. Bees and returning tame-wild animals require distinct control boundaries rather than a free nearest-reference rule.

rivals.R_ANY_ESCAPE_LOSES: Every escaped animal becomes the first occupant's property; this contradicts domestic fowl and visible/easy-pursuit swarms.
rivals.R_WOUND_OWNS: Severe wounding plus continued pursuit creates ownership before seizure; this is the rejected Trebatius opinion, not the confirmed Institutes rule.
rivals.R_CONTROL_ONLY: All ownership follows visibility/pursuit regardless of animal nature; this loses the source's wild/domestic and return-intention distinctions.

falsifier: Reject the constructor if a complete source passage uses one escape/pursuit rule without the source's nature, enclosure, or return-intention distinctions, or if the adopted no-ownership-before-seizure rule cannot be kept separate from Trebatius' explicitly rejected opinion. A target application would require independently bound nature, control event, and later occupant roles; assigning them occurrence by occurrence would remove the proposed discriminator.
dependencies: Animal names and owner names are opaque source variables; no target word or manuscript meaning is assigned.
Physical identity of the animal is preserved across escape; ownership/reference changes are event-scoped, not new animal creation.
The source's legal nature categories are assumed as typed fields for this exploratory constructor; they are not claimed to be manuscript categories.
The complete source account includes all clauses in II.12–16, including land-entry prohibition, honey, hive enclosure, return habit, and theft consequence.
